domain.title: AI Risk, Impact & Assurance
domain.outcome: Integrate D03 knowledge into defensible AI-governance analysis, professional artifacts and accountable decisions.

modules.title: Foundations of AI Risk
modules.whyThisMatters: Without a shared vocabulary, organizations confuse compliance with safety, scores with truth, and incidents with the full range of foreseeable harm.
learningObjectives: Define AI risk and distinguish it from uncertainty, harm, impact, compliance and incident; explain distinctive technical and social risk; assign owners and appetite; connect governance, controls, assurance, monitoring and incident management.

contentSections.label: Overview
contentSections.content: AI risk management is the disciplined practice of understanding possible adverse effects of AI-enabled systems and deciding how to prevent, reduce, monitor, accept or escalate them.

content.explanation: AI risk is analyzed through the complete chain of source, event, vulnerability, consequence, affected stakeholder, control, evidence and review. The term is not a conclusion by itself; its meaning depends on system purpose, lifecycle stage, context and available evidence.
content.example: A Bangladesh-based digital lender uses an AI recommendation to prioritize applications; applicants may have limited ability to challenge an adverse outcome.
content.governance_implication: The risk owner records the reasoning, identifies uncertainty, and selects controls proportionate to severity, exposure, reversibility, rights and safety implications.
content.professional_application: Apply AI risk in an intake review, risk register, impact assessment, control decision or executive escalation.

contentSections.label: Governance practice
content: Define purpose, system boundary, stakeholders, assets, lifecycle stage and decision authority before assessing risk.
Use qualitative and quantitative evidence together; record confidence, missing data, dissenting views and limitations.
For resource-constrained teams, prioritize consequential decisions, vulnerable groups, safety-critical functions and irreversible harms, while using reusable templates and vendor evidence.

contentSections.label: Worked examples
content: A Bangladesh-based digital lender uses an AI recommendation to prioritize applications; applicants may have limited ability to challenge an adverse outcome.
A Kenyan public-health service uses a multilingual triage assistant hosted by a foreign cloud provider; connectivity and local-language data are uneven.
A Latin American university uses generative AI to support admissions and student services; staff may over-trust fluent outputs.

activities: Map Governance → Risk Management → Controls → Assurance → Monitoring → Incident Management for one AI service.
Draft a risk appetite, tolerance, acceptance and escalation record for a consequential use case.

cases.title: The fluent triage assistant
cases.context: The organization operates with mixed technical capacity, vendor dependency and unequal access to remediation.
cases.ai_system: A multilingual AI system supporting recommendations or consequential workflow decisions.
cases.risk_problem: A confident but wrong recommendation could delay care, while a low-frequency failure affects a vulnerable group.
evidence_facts: purpose and system boundary are documented
performance varies across language, region or subgroup
vendor evidence is incomplete
human review exists but capacity is limited
cases.decision_point: Whether to limit recommendations to decision support and require clinical confirmation.
cases.analysis: Separate risk source, event, vulnerability and consequence. Examine likelihood, severity, exposure, reversibility, detectability, rights, safety, systemic effects and uncertainty.
cases.governance_response: Pause or constrain the affected function where necessary; assign an owner; gather missing evidence; consult affected groups; implement technical, operational and human controls; document residual risk and escalation.
cases.lessons_learned: A risk decision is defensible when it explains what is known, what is uncertain, who may be harmed, what controls exist, and why the decision remains proportionate.

knowledgeChecks.question: A model has a low probability of severe harm. What is the best response?
options: Document assumptions and evidence before deciding
Use a score without reviewing context
Delegate accountability to the vendor
Ignore low-probability severe harm

knowledgeChecks.explanation: A defensible AI risk decision links facts, assumptions, stakeholders, method, uncertainty, controls and ownership.
knowledgeChecks.rationale: This prevents numerical or organizational shortcuts from replacing professional risk reasoning.

contentSections.label: Governance practice
content: Define purpose, system boundary, stakeholders, assets, lifecycle stage and decision authority before assessing risk.
Use qualitative and quantitative evidence together; record confidence, missing data, dissenting views and limitations.
For resource-constrained teams, prioritize consequential decisions, vulnerable groups, safety-critical functions and irreversible harms, while using reusable templates and vendor evidence.

cases.title: The invisible boundary
cases.context: The organization operates with mixed technical capacity, vendor dependency and unequal access to remediation.
cases.ai_system: A multilingual AI system supporting recommendations or consequential workflow decisions.
cases.risk_problem: A recommendation engine is connected to a credit workflow, but the documented boundary excludes downstream human decisions.
evidence_facts: purpose and system boundary are documented
performance varies across language, region or subgroup
vendor evidence is incomplete
human review exists but capacity is limited
cases.decision_point: Whether downstream effects belong in identification and who must participate.
cases.analysis: Separate risk source, event, vulnerability and consequence. Examine likelihood, severity, exposure, reversibility, detectability, rights, safety, systemic effects and uncertainty.
cases.governance_response: Pause or constrain the affected function where necessary; assign an owner; gather missing evidence; consult affected groups; implement technical, operational and human controls; document residual risk and escalation.
cases.lessons_learned: A risk decision is defensible when it explains what is known, what is uncertain, who may be harmed, what controls exist, and why the decision remains proportionate.

modules.whyThisMatters: Classification supports consistent reasoning, but a taxonomy can hide harm when categories are too narrow, mutually exclusive or detached from affected populations and lifecycle context.

contentSections.label: Overview

contentSections.label: Governance practice
content: Define purpose, system boundary, stakeholders, assets, lifecycle stage and decision authority before assessing risk.
Use qualitative and quantitative evidence together; record confidence, missing data, dissenting views and limitations.
For resource-constrained teams, prioritize consequential decisions, vulnerable groups, safety-critical functions and irreversible harms, while using reusable templates and vendor evidence.

contentSections.label: Worked examples
content: A Bangladesh-based digital lender uses an AI recommendation to prioritize applications; applicants may have limited ability to challenge an adverse outcome.
A Kenyan public-health service uses a multilingual triage assistant hosted by a foreign cloud provider; connectivity and local-language data are uneven.
A Latin American university uses generative AI to support admissions and student services; staff may over-trust fluent outputs.

activities: Design an AI Risk Taxonomy and crosswalk it to governance domains.
Convert an unstructured risk register into structured taxonomy records with owners, evidence and indicators.

cases.title: One risk, many categories
cases.context: The organization operates with mixed technical capacity, vendor dependency and unequal access to remediation.
cases.ai_system: A multilingual AI system supporting recommendations or consequential workflow decisions.
cases.risk_problem: A student-ranking system creates privacy, equality, reputational and educational risks at different lifecycle stages.
evidence_facts: purpose and system boundary are documented
performance varies across language, region or subgroup
vendor evidence is incomplete
human review exists but capacity is limited
cases.decision_point: Whether to classify by lifecycle, impact, rights, sector or a hybrid structure.
cases.analysis: Separate risk source, event, vulnerability and consequence. Examine likelihood, severity, exposure, reversibility, detectability, rights, safety, systemic effects and uncertainty.
cases.governance_response: Pause or constrain the affected function where necessary; assign an owner; gather missing evidence; consult affected groups; implement technical, operational and human controls; document residual risk and escalation.
cases.lessons_learned: A risk decision is defensible when it explains what is known, what is uncertain, who may be harmed, what controls exist, and why the decision remains proportionate.

modules.title: AI Impact Assessment
modules.whyThisMatters: A model can be technically functional yet harmful in context. Impact assessment makes affected people visible and requires consultation, mitigation, approval and post-deployment review.
learningObjectives: Distinguish risk and impact assessments; integrate privacy, data protection, human-rights, algorithmic, social, environmental, equality, security and safety assessments; assess before, during and after deployment; conduct meaningful consultation.

contentSections.label: Overview
contentSections.content: An AI Impact Assessment examines how an AI system may affect people, organizations, communities and the environment, including benefits, harms, distribution, rights, participation and residual effects.

contentSections.label: Governance practice
content: Define purpose, system boundary, stakeholders, assets, lifecycle stage and decision authority before assessing risk.
Use qualitative and quantitative evidence together; record confidence, missing data, dissenting views and limitations.
For resource-constrained teams, prioritize consequential decisions, vulnerable groups, safety-critical functions and irreversible harms, while using reusable templates and vendor evidence.

contentSections.label: Worked examples
content: A Bangladesh-based digital lender uses an AI recommendation to prioritize applications; applicants may have limited ability to challenge an adverse outcome.
A Kenyan public-health service uses a multilingual triage assistant hosted by a foreign cloud provider; connectivity and local-language data are uneven.
A Latin American university uses generative AI to support admissions and student services; staff may over-trust fluent outputs.

activities: Complete an AI Impact Assessment for a public-service recommender, including consultation and residual impacts.
Map how privacy, human-rights, equality, safety and environmental assessments interact without duplicating evidence.

cases.title: The queue that changed lives
cases.context: The organization operates with mixed technical capacity, vendor dependency and unequal access to remediation.
cases.ai_system: A multilingual AI system supporting recommendations or consequential workflow decisions.
cases.risk_problem: An eligibility recommender changes service order and affects people with limited documentation or connectivity.
evidence_facts: purpose and system boundary are documented
performance varies across language, region or subgroup
vendor evidence is incomplete
human review exists but capacity is limited
cases.decision_point: Whether the system can proceed, with what consultation, safeguards and alternative access.
cases.analysis: Separate risk source, event, vulnerability and consequence. Examine likelihood, severity, exposure, reversibility, detectability, rights, safety, systemic effects and uncertainty.
cases.governance_response: Pause or constrain the affected function where necessary; assign an owner; gather missing evidence; consult affected groups; implement technical, operational and human controls; document residual risk and escalation.
cases.lessons_learned: A risk decision is defensible when it explains what is known, what is uncertain, who may be harmed, what controls exist, and why the decision remains proportionate.

modules.title: Risk Assessment Methodologies
modules.whyThisMatters: Organizations need decisions that are reproducible enough to review yet humble enough to show assumptions, uncertainty, confidence and limits.
learningObjectives: Select qualitative, quantitative or hybrid methods; use probability, severity, exposure, expected loss, scoring, confidence and sensitivity analysis; explain risk matrices and their limitations; document assumptions, evidence, reviewer, owner, decision, residual risk and escalation.

contentSections.label: Overview
contentSections.content: Risk assessment methodology provides a transparent route from identification to analysis, evaluation, treatment, residual-risk decision and monitoring. It is a reasoning aid, not an oracle.

contentSections.label: Governance practice
content: Define purpose, system boundary, stakeholders, assets, lifecycle stage and decision authority before assessing risk.
Use qualitative and quantitative evidence together; record confidence, missing data, dissenting views and limitations.
For resource-constrained teams, prioritize consequential decisions, vulnerable groups, safety-critical functions and irreversible harms, while using reusable templates and vendor evidence.

cases.title: The misleading green score
cases.context: The organization operates with mixed technical capacity, vendor dependency and unequal access to remediation.
cases.ai_system: A multilingual AI system supporting recommendations or consequential workflow decisions.
cases.risk_problem: A weighted matrix labels a low-frequency, high-severity exclusion risk as medium because averages dilute subgroup harm.
evidence_facts: purpose and system boundary are documented
performance varies across language, region or subgroup
vendor evidence is incomplete
human review exists but capacity is limited
cases.decision_point: Whether to accept the score or override it with rights, severity, uncertainty and vulnerability analysis.
cases.analysis: Separate risk source, event, vulnerability and consequence. Examine likelihood, severity, exposure, reversibility, detectability, rights, safety, systemic effects and uncertainty.
cases.governance_response: Pause or constrain the affected function where necessary; assign an owner; gather missing evidence; consult affected groups; implement technical, operational and human controls; document residual risk and escalation.
cases.lessons_learned: A risk decision is defensible when it explains what is known, what is uncertain, who may be harmed, what controls exist, and why the decision remains proportionate.

modules.title: Risk Scoring & Prioritization
modules.whyThisMatters: Leaders need to decide what must be treated first when resources are limited. A score can help sequence work, but it can also hide severe, systemic, cascading or rights-sensitive harm.
learningObjectives: Define scoring purpose; select likelihood, severity, exposure and contextual factors; design qualitative, semi-quantitative and quantitative approaches; analyze sensitivity and uncertainty; set appetite and escalation thresholds; produce six scoring artifacts.

contentSections.label: Overview
contentSections.content: Risk scoring organizes evidence for decision support, but it must not turn contested assumptions into false certainty. This module teaches learners to compare, rank and prioritize risks while preserving context, vulnerability and uncertainty.

contentSections.label: Governance practice
content: Define purpose, scope, criteria, decision authority and evidence expectations before selecting a method or accepting a result.
Use proportionate implementation: prioritize consequential uses, vulnerable populations, safety/security risks and irreversible or systemic effects.

In Bangladesh, South Asia, Africa, Southeast Asia and Latin America, adapt methods to local language, connectivity, data availability, specialist capacity and vendor dependence without removing essential safeguards.

cases.title: The green heat map
cases.context: A resource-constrained organization depends on external vendors, cloud infrastructure and local-language or subgroup evidence.
cases.ai_system: A multilingual AI system supporting consequential recommendations, controls, testing and evidence review.
cases.governance_risk_problem: A weighted matrix makes a severe language-minority exclusion risk appear medium because subgroup exposure and irreversibility are not represented.
evidence: system purpose and boundary are documented
aggregate vendor metrics are available but subgroup evidence is incomplete
human review and monitoring capacity are limited
model or configuration changes may occur
cases.decision_point: Whether to override the ranking, gather evidence, restrict deployment or accept residual risk.
cases.analysis: Assess scope, assumptions, evidence quality, uncertainty, affected populations, independence, control effectiveness, test coverage and residual risk. Avoid treating any score, test, assurance statement or record as complete proof outside its defined scope.
cases.response: Define the decision and criteria; assign accountable owners; gather or generate evidence; apply proportionate controls and testing; record limitations, exceptions, management response, residual risk and review date.
cases.lessons_learned: A professional conclusion states what was examined, against which criteria, with what evidence, by whom, with what limitations, and what happens next.

content: Define purpose, scope, criteria, decision authority and evidence expectations before selecting a method or accepting a result.
Use proportionate implementation: prioritize consequential uses, vulnerable populations, safety/security risks and irreversible or systemic effects.

In Bangladesh, South Asia, Africa, Southeast Asia and Latin America, adapt methods to local language, connectivity, data availability, specialist capacity and vendor dependence without removing essential safeguards.

cases.title: The control without an owner
cases.context: A resource-constrained organization depends on external vendors, cloud infrastructure and local-language or subgroup evidence.
cases.ai_system: A multilingual AI system supporting consequential recommendations, controls, testing and evidence review.
cases.governance_risk_problem: A human-oversight policy exists, but no one tracks overrides, workload or what happens when the reviewer disagrees.
evidence: system purpose and boundary are documented
aggregate vendor metrics are available but subgroup evidence is incomplete
human review and monitoring capacity are limited
model or configuration changes may occur
cases.decision_point: Whether the control is designed, evidenced and effective enough for continued use.
cases.analysis: Assess scope, assumptions, evidence quality, uncertainty, affected populations, independence, control effectiveness, test coverage and residual risk. Avoid treating any score, test, assurance statement or record as complete proof outside its defined scope.
cases.response: Define the decision and criteria; assign accountable owners; gather or generate evidence; apply proportionate controls and testing; record limitations, exceptions, management response, residual risk and review date.
cases.lessons_learned: A professional conclusion states what was examined, against which criteria, with what evidence, by whom, with what limitations, and what happens next.

modules.title: AI Assurance Concepts
modules.whyThisMatters: Organizations need to communicate what has been examined, against which criteria, with what evidence and limitations. Assurance helps decision-makers avoid unsupported claims while preserving independence and competence.
learningObjectives: Define AI assurance; distinguish internal, external, first-, second- and third-party assurance; set scope, objectives and criteria; evaluate evidence; manage independence, competence, objectivity, transparency, confidence and limitations; follow the assurance lifecycle.

contentSections.label: Overview
contentSections.content: AI assurance provides a structured, evidence-based basis for confidence about defined claims. It is related to governance, risk management, compliance, testing and audit, but is not identical to any of them.

contentSections.label: Governance practice
content: Define purpose, scope, criteria, decision authority and evidence expectations before selecting a method or accepting a result.
Use proportionate implementation: prioritize consequential uses, vulnerable populations, safety/security risks and irreversible or systemic effects.

In Bangladesh, South Asia, Africa, Southeast Asia and Latin America, adapt methods to local language, connectivity, data availability, specialist capacity and vendor dependence without removing essential safeguards.

cases.title: The certificate that proved too much
cases.context: A resource-constrained organization depends on external vendors, cloud infrastructure and local-language or subgroup evidence.
cases.ai_system: A multilingual AI system supporting consequential recommendations, controls, testing and evidence review.
cases.governance_risk_problem: A vendor certificate covers a management process but is presented as proof of clinical safety and fairness for a new deployment.
evidence: system purpose and boundary are documented
aggregate vendor metrics are available but subgroup evidence is incomplete
human review and monitoring capacity are limited
model or configuration changes may occur
cases.decision_point: How to scope an assurance conclusion and communicate limitations.
cases.analysis: Assess scope, assumptions, evidence quality, uncertainty, affected populations, independence, control effectiveness, test coverage and residual risk. Avoid treating any score, test, assurance statement or record as complete proof outside its defined scope.
cases.response: Define the decision and criteria; assign accountable owners; gather or generate evidence; apply proportionate controls and testing; record limitations, exceptions, management response, residual risk and review date.
cases.lessons_learned: A professional conclusion states what was examined, against which criteria, with what evidence, by whom, with what limitations, and what happens next.

modules.title: Testing, Validation & Evaluation
modules.whyThisMatters: A system may pass a benchmark and still fail in a language, subgroup, adversarial scenario, tool-use pathway or changed deployment. Good evaluation makes coverage, uncertainty, errors and limits visible.
learningObjectives: Distinguish testing, validation and evaluation; design pre- and post-deployment tests; cover function, performance, safety, security, robustness, reliability, fairness, privacy, factuality, explainability, oversight, adversarial behavior, red teaming, stress, boundary, failure, regression, change and user acceptance; document metrics and uncertainty.

contentSections.label: Overview
contentSections.content: Testing, validation and evaluation produce evidence about whether an AI system meets defined criteria under defined conditions. They are governance activities, not merely engineering tasks.

contentSections.label: Governance practice
content: Define purpose, scope, criteria, decision authority and evidence expectations before selecting a method or accepting a result.
Use proportionate implementation: prioritize consequential uses, vulnerable populations, safety/security risks and irreversible or systemic effects.

In Bangladesh, South Asia, Africa, Southeast Asia and Latin America, adapt methods to local language, connectivity, data availability, specialist capacity and vendor dependence without removing essential safeguards.

cases.title: The benchmark passed, the service failed
cases.context: A resource-constrained organization depends on external vendors, cloud infrastructure and local-language or subgroup evidence.
cases.ai_system: A multilingual AI system supporting consequential recommendations, controls, testing and evidence review.
cases.governance_risk_problem: Aggregate accuracy passed, but the system generated unsupported claims and inconsistent outputs in local languages after a model change.
evidence: system purpose and boundary are documented
aggregate vendor metrics are available but subgroup evidence is incomplete
human review and monitoring capacity are limited
model or configuration changes may occur
cases.decision_point: Whether to release, roll back, constrain or expand evaluation.
cases.analysis: Assess scope, assumptions, evidence quality, uncertainty, affected populations, independence, control effectiveness, test coverage and residual risk. Avoid treating any score, test, assurance statement or record as complete proof outside its defined scope.
cases.response: Define the decision and criteria; assign accountable owners; gather or generate evidence; apply proportionate controls and testing; record limitations, exceptions, management response, residual risk and review date.
cases.lessons_learned: A professional conclusion states what was examined, against which criteria, with what evidence, by whom, with what limitations, and what happens next.

modules.title: Auditability & Evidence
modules.whyThisMatters: Without evidence, an organization cannot show that risks were prioritized, controls operated, assurance criteria were applied or testing was completed. Auditability connects claims to records across the AI lifecycle.
learningObjectives: Distinguish auditability, transparency and explainability; design audit trails; manage evidence integrity, provenance, retention, version control, decision logs, model/system, data, change, approval, risk, control, testing, incident, monitoring and vendor records; apply the evidence lifecycle.

content: Define purpose, scope, criteria, decision authority and evidence expectations before selecting a method or accepting a result.
Use proportionate implementation: prioritize consequential uses, vulnerable populations, safety/security risks and irreversible or systemic effects.

In Bangladesh, South Asia, Africa, Southeast Asia and Latin America, adapt methods to local language, connectivity, data availability, specialist capacity and vendor dependence without removing essential safeguards.

cases.title: The missing deployment decision
cases.context: A resource-constrained organization depends on external vendors, cloud infrastructure and local-language or subgroup evidence.
cases.ai_system: A multilingual AI system supporting consequential recommendations, controls, testing and evidence review.
cases.governance_risk_problem: The organization has test results and policies but cannot show which model version was approved or who accepted residual risk.
evidence: system purpose and boundary are documented
aggregate vendor metrics are available but subgroup evidence is incomplete
human review and monitoring capacity are limited
model or configuration changes may occur
cases.decision_point: Whether evidence can be reconstructed and what remediation is required.
cases.analysis: Assess scope, assumptions, evidence quality, uncertainty, affected populations, independence, control effectiveness, test coverage and residual risk. Avoid treating any score, test, assurance statement or record as complete proof outside its defined scope.
cases.response: Define the decision and criteria; assign accountable owners; gather or generate evidence; apply proportionate controls and testing; record limitations, exceptions, management response, residual risk and review date.
cases.lessons_learned: A professional conclusion states what was examined, against which criteria, with what evidence, by whom, with what limitations, and what happens next.

modules.title: Model Risk & System Risk
modules.whyThisMatters: A model can be accurate in isolation and still create system failure through interfaces, automation bias, infrastructure dependency, vendor updates or cascading effects.
learningObjectives: Distinguish model and system risk; analyze limitations, drift, instability, generalization, misuse, dependency, integration, human interaction and systemic effects; govern foundation models, retrieval, tools, chaining, routing, agents and updates; produce eight artifacts.

contentSections.label: Overview
contentSections.content: Model risk arises from limitations, assumptions, data interaction, performance and change in a model. System risk arises from the wider environment in which the model is integrated, operated and relied upon.

contentSections.label: Governance practice
content: Define the system boundary, actors, dependencies, decision rights and evidence standard before accepting a claim.
Use proportionate governance: prioritize consequential uses, vulnerable groups, safety/security concerns, irreversible harms and material dependencies.
Where budgets and expertise are limited, reuse templates, require vendor evidence contractually, use shared assurance and escalate uncertainty rather than silently accepting it.

content: A Bangladesh service uses a foreign foundation model through an API; a version change alters factuality and tool-use behavior, so model risk and integration risk are recorded separately.
A Kenyan public agency cannot independently inspect a vendor model, so it strengthens boundary mapping, contractual evidence, local monitoring, human review and exit planning.

cases.title: The accurate model that failed the service
cases.context: The organization operates with limited specialist capacity, external vendors, cloud dependency and uneven local-language or subgroup evidence.
cases.ai_system: A complex AI-enabled service with foundation-model dependencies, integrations, monitoring and consequential outputs.
cases.governance_risk_problem: A model passes benchmark tests but its interface encourages clinicians to accept recommendations without checking missing context.
evidence: purpose and model/system boundary are documented
aggregate vendor evidence is stronger than local contextual evidence
model or vendor updates occur periodically
human review and incident records are incomplete
cases.decision_point: Whether to redesign the interface, restrict use, add human controls or accept residual risk.
cases.analysis: Distinguish model from system risk; identify dependencies and affected people; evaluate controls, residual risk, authority, evidence quality, uncertainty and change triggers.
cases.response: Define scope and criteria; assign accountable owners; gather missing evidence; constrain or pause risky functions where necessary; implement controls; test and assure; document acceptance or escalation; monitor and review.
cases.lessons_learned: Risk decisions should explain what is known, uncertain, controlled, accepted, escalated and subject to reassessment.

modules.title: Third-Party & Supply-Chain AI Risk
modules.whyThisMatters: Outsourcing a function does not erase the deployer’s governance responsibility. Supply-chain failure, opaque updates, concentration and weak exit options can undermine otherwise strong controls.
learningObjectives: Identify supply-chain actors and dependencies; conduct vendor, capability, security, privacy, governance and regulatory due diligence; review provenance, testing, assurance, incidents and resilience; design contractual governance, monitoring and exit plans.

contentSections.label: Governance practice
content: Define the system boundary, actors, dependencies, decision rights and evidence standard before accepting a claim.
Use proportionate governance: prioritize consequential uses, vulnerable groups, safety/security concerns, irreversible harms and material dependencies.
Where budgets and expertise are limited, reuse templates, require vendor evidence contractually, use shared assurance and escalate uncertainty rather than silently accepting it.

A Kenyan public agency cannot independently inspect a vendor model, so it strengthens boundary mapping, contractual evidence, local monitoring, human review and exit planning.
A Latin American platform accepts limited residual risk only after documenting affected groups, compensating controls, authority, expiry date and continuous-assurance triggers.

cases.title: The vendor chain no one mapped
cases.context: The organization operates with limited specialist capacity, external vendors, cloud dependency and uneven local-language or subgroup evidence.
cases.ai_system: A complex AI-enabled service with foundation-model dependencies, integrations, monitoring and consequential outputs.
cases.governance_risk_problem: A credit API depends on a cloud region, foundation model, data broker and undisclosed subprocessor; an incident exposes uncertainty about notification and responsibility.
evidence: purpose and model/system boundary are documented
aggregate vendor evidence is stronger than local contextual evidence
model or vendor updates occur periodically
human review and incident records are incomplete
cases.decision_point: Whether to continue, constrain, renegotiate, diversify or exit.
cases.analysis: Distinguish model from system risk; identify dependencies and affected people; evaluate controls, residual risk, authority, evidence quality, uncertainty and change triggers.
cases.response: Define scope and criteria; assign accountable owners; gather missing evidence; constrain or pause risky functions where necessary; implement controls; test and assure; document acceptance or escalation; monitor and review.
cases.lessons_learned: Risk decisions should explain what is known, uncertain, controlled, accepted, escalated and subject to reassessment.

modules.title: Residual Risk & Risk Acceptance
modules.whyThisMatters: Every deployment leaves uncertainty and imperfect controls. Professionals must explain what remains, who can accept it, under what conditions, for how long and when escalation is mandatory.
learningObjectives: Analyze inherent, target and residual risk; evaluate control effectiveness, uncertainty, evidence, stakeholders, reversibility, rights, safety and systemic effects; distinguish avoid, reduce, transfer, accept, defer, redesign and discontinue; document authority and review.

contentSections.label: Overview
contentSections.content: Residual risk is the risk remaining after controls and treatment. Risk acceptance is a structured authority decision, not a default response to limited resources.

contentSections.label: Governance practice
content: Define the system boundary, actors, dependencies, decision rights and evidence standard before accepting a claim.
Use proportionate governance: prioritize consequential uses, vulnerable groups, safety/security concerns, irreversible harms and material dependencies.
Where budgets and expertise are limited, reuse templates, require vendor evidence contractually, use shared assurance and escalate uncertainty rather than silently accepting it.

cases.title: The acceptance that expired
cases.context: The organization operates with limited specialist capacity, external vendors, cloud dependency and uneven local-language or subgroup evidence.
cases.ai_system: A complex AI-enabled service with foundation-model dependencies, integrations, monitoring and consequential outputs.
cases.governance_risk_problem: An executive accepted residual risk for three months while a compensating control was built, but no review occurred after evidence worsened.
evidence: purpose and model/system boundary are documented
aggregate vendor evidence is stronger than local contextual evidence
model or vendor updates occur periodically
human review and incident records are incomplete
cases.decision_point: Whether the acceptance remains valid and who must act.
cases.analysis: Distinguish model from system risk; identify dependencies and affected people; evaluate controls, residual risk, authority, evidence quality, uncertainty and change triggers.
cases.response: Define scope and criteria; assign accountable owners; gather missing evidence; constrain or pause risky functions where necessary; implement controls; test and assure; document acceptance or escalation; monitor and review.
cases.lessons_learned: Risk decisions should explain what is known, uncertain, controlled, accepted, escalated and subject to reassessment.

modules.title: Continuous Assurance
modules.whyThisMatters: Initial approval becomes stale when models, data, vendors, regulations, users or operating conditions change. Continuous assurance creates a repeatable lifecycle rather than a one-time certificate.
learningObjectives: Design continuous monitoring and assurance; select risk-based frequency; define event and periodic triggers; monitor performance, drift, fairness, safety, security, privacy, factuality, complaints, incidents, overrides, vendor and system changes; operate the assurance lifecycle.

contentSections.label: Governance practice
content: Define the system boundary, actors, dependencies, decision rights and evidence standard before accepting a claim.
Use proportionate governance: prioritize consequential uses, vulnerable groups, safety/security concerns, irreversible harms and material dependencies.
Where budgets and expertise are limited, reuse templates, require vendor evidence contractually, use shared assurance and escalate uncertainty rather than silently accepting it.

contentSections.label: Worked examples
content: A Bangladesh service uses a foreign foundation model through an API; a version change alters factuality and tool-use behavior, so model risk and integration risk are recorded separately.

A Latin American platform accepts limited residual risk only after documenting affected groups, compensating controls, authority, expiry date and continuous-assurance triggers.

activities: Build a Continuous Assurance Plan and Assurance Monitoring Framework with baselines, thresholds, owners and actions.
Create an Assurance Trigger Matrix, Refresh Schedule, Continuous Risk Register, Dashboard Specification and Post-Deployment Review.
